examTakeaway: A wide pulse pressure with a diastolic murmur at the left sternal border is aortic regurgitation, and the head bobbing is stroke volume.
scenario: A 40-year-old man has a blood pressure of 160/50 mm Hg. The carotid pulse rises quickly and collapses. A diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal border when he leans forward. There is no opening snap and no diastolic rumble at the apex in the left lateral position as the main finding. He had a bicuspid valve noted years ago.
question: Which valve lesion is this?
explanation: A wide pulse pressure with a diastolic murmur at the left sternal border is aortic regurgitation, and the head bobbing is stroke volume. Aortic regurgitation lets the stroke volume fall back in diastole, so the diastolic pressure is 50 and the pulse collapses. Aortic stenosis is a systolic ejection murmur with a narrow pulse pressure. Mitral stenosis is a diastolic rumble at the apex with an opening snap, which is not the main finding. Mitral valve prolapse is a mid-systolic click. Pulmonic stenosis is a systolic murmur that does not widen the arm pulse pressure.

examTakeaway: An opening snap and a diastolic rumble in a person who had rheumatic fever are mitral stenosis.
scenario: A 35-year-old woman who had rheumatic fever as a child is short of breath. There is an opening snap after the second heart sound and a low rumble in diastole at the apex, louder in the left lateral position. Blood pressure is 120/80 mm Hg. There is no collapsing carotid pulse.
question: Which valve is narrow?
explanation: An opening snap and a diastolic rumble in a person who had rheumatic fever are mitral stenosis. Mitral valve opening makes the snap, and the rumble is flow across a narrow mitral orifice at the apex. Aortic valve in systole is a crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the right upper sternal border. Aortic valve leaking in diastole widens the pulse pressure, and hers is 120/80. Pulmonic valve stenosis is a systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Tricuspid valve from carcinoid is a right-sided lesion with flushing and a liver metastasis story, not rheumatic fever.

examTakeaway: A fixed split second heart sound and a left-to-right atrial shunt is an atrial septal defect, not a VSD.
scenario: A 25-year-old woman has mild shortness of breath. The second heart sound stays split on inspiration and expiration. There is a soft systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. The murmur is not holosystolic at the left lower border and there is no thrill. ECG shows an incomplete right bundle pattern.
question: Which shunt is this?
explanation: A fixed split second heart sound and a left-to-right atrial shunt is an atrial septal defect, not a VSD. Atrial septal defect overloads the right ventricle in both phases of breathing, so the split does not close. Ventricular septal defect is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, often with a thrill, which is absent. Patent ductus arteriosus is a continuous machine murmur. Tetralogy of Fallot presents with cyanosis in infancy. Coarctation causes higher pressure in the arms than the legs.

examTakeaway: A mid-systolic click that moves earlier when she stands is mitral valve prolapse, because less preload lets the leaflet slip sooner.
scenario: A 23-year-old woman has a mid-systolic click at the apex. When she stands up, the click moves closer to the first heart sound and a short murmur appears. When she squats, the click moves later. She has no diastolic rumble and the pulse pressure is normal. There is no family history of sudden death on the field.
question: Which valve motion is the click?
options: A mitral leaflet slipping into the atrium
An opening snap of mitral stenosis
correctAnswer: A mitral leaflet slipping into the atrium
explanation: A mid-systolic click that moves earlier when she stands is mitral valve prolapse, because less preload lets the leaflet slip sooner. A mitral leaflet slipping into the atrium happens earlier when standing shrinks the ventricle and later when squatting fills it. Dynamic outflow obstruction gets louder with Valsalva and comes with a family history of sudden death, which she does not have. An opening snap of mitral stenosis is diastolic. Aortic ejection is a systolic murmur at the base that does not click and move with squat. A pericardial knock is early diastole in constriction.

examTakeaway: Pulmonary edema and a new apical holosystolic murmur on day 3 after infarction, without a sternal thrill, is papillary muscle rupture.
scenario: A 64-year-old man is day 3 after an inferior infarction. He suddenly cannot breathe. A new holosystolic murmur is loudest at the apex and radiates to the axilla. There is no thrill at the left sternal border. The lungs are full of rales. Blood pressure is 90/60 mm Hg.
question: Which structure tore?
options: The free wall into the pericardium
explanation: Pulmonary edema and a new apical holosystolic murmur on day 3 after infarction, without a sternal thrill, is papillary muscle rupture. A papillary muscle lets the mitral leaflet flail, so the murmur is apical and the lungs flood. The interventricular septum rupture is also holosystolic but usually has a thrill at the left sternal border, which is absent. The free wall into the pericardium causes tamponade and electromechanical dissociation, not an apical murmur into the axilla. A coronary artery plaque only is the original infarction, not a new regurgitant murmur. The atrial septum is not the post-infarct tear.

examTakeaway: Inferior ST elevation with bradycardia is the right coronary artery, which also feeds the AV node in most people.
scenario: A 60-year-old man has chest pain. ST segments are elevated in leads II, III, and aVF, and lead III is higher than lead II. Heart rate is 42 bpm with a narrow complex. Blood pressure is 130/80 mm Hg. There is no ST elevation in V2 through V4.
question: Which artery is closed?
options: Left circumflex artery as the only anterior vessel
explanation: Inferior ST elevation with bradycardia is the right coronary artery, which also feeds the AV node in most people. Right coronary artery occlusion lifts II, III, and aVF and can slow the node. Left anterior descending artery lifts V2 through V4, which are not elevated. Left circumflex artery as the only anterior vessel more often lifts the lateral leads. The left main trunk is a broad disaster, not an isolated inferior pattern with a stable pressure. A diagonal branch only is a limited anterior or lateral change.

examTakeaway: A pericardial knock, ascites, and a jugular vein that rises on inspiration are constriction, not tamponade.
scenario: A 50-year-old man treated for tuberculosis years ago has leg swelling and ascites. There is an early diastolic sound. The jugular venous pressure rises when he inhales. Pulsus paradoxus is absent. The heart is not enlarged and there was no recent stab wound.
question: Which pericardial state is this?
explanation: A pericardial knock, ascites, and a jugular vein that rises on inspiration are constriction, not tamponade. Constriction blocks filling and the knock is the sudden halt, and Kussmaul rise on inspiration is typical. Tamponade has pulsus paradoxus and a falling pressure after a wound or a bleed, which he does not have. Fibrinous pericarditis of week one is a rub and pain, not years of ascites. A large pleural effusion does not make a knock or Kussmaul sign. Restrictive cardiomyopathy only can look similar, but the old tuberculosis and the knock point at the pericardium.

examTakeaway: A ventricular septal defect that was pink and is now blue, with a quieter murmur, has reversed because pulmonary resistance exceeded systemic.
scenario: A 17-year-old who had a loud holosystolic murmur as a child is now cyanotic and clubbed. The murmur is much softer. The right ventricle is hypertrophied. He was never a blue infant who squatted, and the chest film does not show a boot-shaped heart from infancy.
question: What happened to the shunt?
options: It is tetralogy that was missed
It reversed because lung resistance rose
correctAnswer: It reversed because lung resistance rose
explanation: A ventricular septal defect that was pink and is now blue, with a quieter murmur, has reversed because pulmonary resistance exceeded systemic. It reversed because lung resistance rose, so flow now goes right to left and the murmur softens as the pressure gap shrinks. It closed on its own would remove the cyanosis, not create it. It became a ductus is a different vessel. It is tetralogy that was missed presents with cyanosis in infancy and squatting, which he did not do. It is isolated pulmonic stenosis is a systolic murmur without this late cyanosis after a childhood VSD.

examTakeaway: An S3 in a dilated ventricle is volume overload, while an S4 is a stiff ventricle squeezing into a noncompliant chamber.
scenario: A 60-year-old man with a large dilated heart has a low-pitched sound just after the second heart sound, heard best at the apex in the left lateral position. He is short of breath and the lungs are wet. There is no sound just before the first heart sound. He is not a healthy young athlete.
question: Which filling sound is this?
options: An S4 of a stiff ventricle
An S3 of a volume-overloaded ventricle
correctAnswer: An S3 of a volume-overloaded ventricle
explanation: An S3 in a dilated ventricle is volume overload, while an S4 is a stiff ventricle squeezing into a noncompliant chamber. An S3 of a volume-overloaded ventricle comes just after S2 as blood rushes into a floppy chamber, and his lungs are wet. An S4 of a stiff ventricle comes just before S1, which was not heard. An opening snap is mitral stenosis and is higher pitched, followed by a rumble. A pericardial knock is earlier and goes with constriction. A tumor plop is a mobile atrial myxoma, with positional symptoms he does not have.

examTakeaway: Epigastric pain that wakes him and is relieved by food is a duodenal ulcer, and the usual driver is H. pylori.
scenario: A 40-year-old man wakes at night with epigastric pain that eases when he eats. He is not on an NSAID. Stool is negative for blood. Pain gets worse when the stomach is empty, not right after a meal. He has no weight loss and the mass in the neck is not present.
question: Which ulcer site fits the food relief?
options: A gastric cancer on the greater curve
explanation: Epigastric pain that wakes him and is relieved by food is a duodenal ulcer, and the usual driver is H. pylori. Duodenal bulb acid hits the ulcer when the stomach is empty, and food buffers it. Gastric body, worse with food, hurts when acid and food arrive. A gastric cancer on the greater curve causes weight loss and sometimes a node, which he does not have. Esophageal varices bleed, they do not wake him with pain relieved by food. A Meckel diverticulum is painless bleeding in a child.

examTakeaway: Flushing and a right-sided valve lesion, with a small-bowel tumor, happen because the lung clears serotonin before the left heart.
scenario: A 55-year-old man has flushing and watery diarrhea. The liver has metastases. The tricuspid valve is thickened and leaking. The mitral valve is normal. Urine 5-HIAA is high. He has no rheumatic history.
question: Why is the left heart spared?
options: Serotonin only injures the tricuspid by chance
The tumor is in the left atrium
explanation: Flushing and a right-sided valve lesion, with a small-bowel tumor, happen because the lung clears serotonin before the left heart. The lung metabolizes serotonin, so once liver metastases let the amine into the hepatic vein and the right heart, the lung removes it before the mitral valve. The tumor is in the left atrium is not this bowel carcinoid. Serotonin only injures the tricuspid by chance ignores the lung filter. The mitral valve is immune is false; it is protected by metabolism. Portal flow skips the liver is the opposite of what metastases do; the metastases are what let serotonin escape the portal bed.

examTakeaway: Painless jaundice and a palpable nontender gallbladder are a pancreatic head cancer, not a stone.
scenario: A 68-year-old man has jaundice and itching without pain. The gallbladder is palpable and nontender. Bilirubin is mostly conjugated. He has lost 8 kg. There is no fever and no colic after fatty meals. Alkaline phosphatase is high.
question: Which duct is blocked?
options: The pancreatic duct by a stone, with a normal bile duct
The intrapancreatic bile duct by a head mass
correctAnswer: The intrapancreatic bile duct by a head mass
explanation: Painless jaundice and a palpable nontender gallbladder are a pancreatic head cancer, not a stone. The intrapancreatic bile duct by a head mass stays blocked long enough for the gallbladder to enlarge, which Courvoisier described. A cystic-duct stone causes biliary colic or cholecystitis, and a chronically inflamed gallbladder usually does not distend painlessly. An intrahepatic duct only would not fill the gallbladder. The pancreatic duct by a stone, with a normal bile duct, would not jaundice him. A colonic mass does not raise conjugated bilirubin.

examTakeaway: Small-bowel obstruction in an older woman with air in the biliary tree is a gallstone that eroded into the gut.
scenario: A 78-year-old woman has crampy pain, vomiting, and a distended abdomen. She had gallstones years ago and no abdominal surgery. The film shows dilated small bowel and air in the biliary tree. There is no fever and the pain is not peritonitis.
question: What is obstructing the bowel?
explanation: Small-bowel obstruction in an older woman with air in the biliary tree is a gallstone that eroded into the gut. A gallstone in the ileum entered through a cholecystenteric fistula, which is why air is in the biliary tree and she has had no operation. Adhesions from a prior operation require surgery she did not have. An inguinal hernia would show a groin mass. Intussusception of the ileum is a child with currant-jelly stool. A volvulus of the sigmoid is large-bowel obstruction with a coffee-bean colon.

examTakeaway: Painless bleeding in a toddler from a vitelline remnant is ectopic gastric mucosa, found with a technetium scan.
scenario: A 2-year-old boy passes a large amount of dark red blood and is otherwise comfortable. The abdomen is soft. He has no currant-jelly stool and no sausage mass. A technetium scan lights up a focus in the right lower quadrant that is not the bladder.
question: Which remnant is bleeding?
explanation: Painless bleeding in a toddler from a vitelline remnant is ectopic gastric mucosa, found with a technetium scan. A Meckel diverticulum holds gastric mucosa that the scan sees and that ulcerates the downstream ileum. Intussusception is intermittent pain and currant-jelly stool with a mass. A juvenile polyp can bleed but does not light up on a Meckel scan. Hirschsprung disease is failure to pass meconium and a distended belly. Midgut volvulus is bilious vomiting in an infant.

examTakeaway: Failure to pass meconium, then a blast of stool after a rectal exam, is absent ganglion cells in the distal colon.
scenario: A 3-day-old boy, a patient in the nursery, has not passed meconium. The belly is distended and he vomits. After a rectal exam a gush of stool comes out. A contrast enema shows a narrow rectum and a dilated colon above it. He does not have a meconium ileus picture of cystic fibrosis as the leading finding, and the sweat test has not been done.
question: Which cells are missing?
options: Ganglion cells of the distal colon
Cajal cells only of the stomach
correctAnswer: Ganglion cells of the distal colon
explanation: Failure to pass meconium, then a blast of stool after a rectal exam, is absent ganglion cells in the distal colon. Ganglion cells of the distal colon failed to migrate, so the rectum stays narrow and the upstream colon dilates. Cajal cells only of the stomach are a motility story higher up, not a narrow rectum. Parietal cells make acid and intrinsic factor. Enterochromaffin cells make serotonin. Pancreatic islet cells make insulin, and their loss is not neonatal obstruction.

examTakeaway: Bloody stool after a hypotensive episode, with pain at the splenic flexure, is watershed ischemia, not mesenteric infarction.
scenario: A 74-year-old man was hypotensive during a bleeding ulcer yesterday. Today he has left-sided cramps and maroon stool. The abdomen is soft and lactate is normal. CT shows thickening at the splenic flexure and the rectum is spared. He does not have pain out of proportion to the exam.
question: Which segment was ischemic?
options: The entire small bowel from the superior mesenteric artery
The rectum, which has a dual supply that failed
A duodenal ulcer that is still the only source
explanation: Bloody stool after a hypotensive episode, with pain at the splenic flexure, is watershed ischemia, not mesenteric infarction. The splenic-flexure watershed sits between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and is hit when pressure falls, while the rectum is spared by dual supply. The entire small bowel from the superior mesenteric artery is pain out of proportion and a rising lactate, which he does not have. The rectum, which has a dual supply that failed, is the opposite of the usual sparing. A duodenal ulcer that is still the only source would be melena without colonic thickening. The cecum from appendicitis is right-sided pain and fever.

examTakeaway: Weight loss, a supraclavicular node, and a stomach that does not distend are signet-ring cells infiltrating the wall.
scenario: A 60-year-old man has lost 10 kg and feels full after a few bites. A hard node sits above the left clavicle. Endoscopy shows a stiff stomach that does not distend, and biopsy shows cells with mucin pushing the nucleus aside. He has no night pain relieved by food as his only symptom.
question: Which cancer pattern is the stiff stomach?
options: MALT lymphoma from H. pylori only
explanation: Weight loss, a supraclavicular node, and a stomach that does not distend are signet-ring cells infiltrating the wall. Linitis plastica from signet-ring cells is that leather-bottle stomach, and the left supraclavicular node is Virchow. A duodenal ulcer hurts at night and is relieved by food, without weight loss as the lead. MALT lymphoma from H. pylori only is a slower lymphoid mass that can regress when the infection is treated. A pancreatic head mass causes painless jaundice. An esophageal squamous cancer causes dysphagia for solids, not early satiety from a stiff stomach.

examTakeaway: A surrogate for a patient who cannot speak uses the patient's known wishes, not the surrogate's own preference.
scenario: A 75-year-old man is unconscious after a stroke. He had told his daughter, and written it down, that he would not want a feeding tube if he could not recover awareness. The daughter now says she cannot bear to stop and asks for the tube. No newer statement from him exists.
question: Whose preference decides?
options: A hospital policy of always feeding
explanation: A surrogate for a patient who cannot speak uses the patient's known wishes, not the surrogate's own preference. The patient's prior written wish is substituted judgment. The daughter's current distress is her feeling, not his decision. The attending physician's habit does not override a known wish. A hospital policy of always feeding cannot erase a valid refusal. The nurse who disagrees is not the decision maker.

examTakeaway: A dosing error caught before the drug reaches the patient is fixed and reported inside the system, and the patient is not told a harm that did not occur.
scenario: A pharmacist catches a tenfold insulin dose on the screen before the syringe is drawn. The patient never received it and is well. The ordering resident wants to hide the near miss from the safety office because nothing happened.
question: Which action fits a miss that never arrived?
options: Report it internally and do not describe a harm
Tell the patient he was injured
Hide it from the safety office
Alter the order so it looks correct from the start
correctAnswer: Report it internally and do not describe a harm
explanation: A dosing error caught before the drug reaches the patient is fixed and reported inside the system, and the patient is not told a harm that did not occur. Report it internally and do not describe a harm keeps the learning and does not invent an injury. Tell the patient he was injured is false. Hide it from the safety office loses the chance to fix the screen. Alter the order so it looks correct from the start destroys the record of the miss. Discharge him to avoid questions abandons the safety report.

examTakeaway: A patient who demands an antibiotic for a clear viral cold is not given one to keep the visit peaceful.
scenario: A 25-year-old man has two days of runny nose, a sore throat, and a cough. He is afebrile. The throat is not exudative and the lungs are clear. He asks for azithromycin so he can return to work tomorrow and says he will be angry without it.
question: Which plan respects the indication?
options: Order a chest film to justify a drug
A steroid pack as a substitute antibiotic
Explain that an antibiotic will not help
correctAnswer: Explain that an antibiotic will not help
explanation: A patient who demands an antibiotic for a clear viral cold is not given one to keep the visit peaceful. Explain that an antibiotic will not help is the indicated plan. Prescribe azithromycin to avoid anger treats the clinician's discomfort. Give penicillin because he insists is the same error. Order a chest film to justify a drug is an unnecessary test. A steroid pack as a substitute antibiotic is not treatment for a simple cold.

examTakeaway: A photo of a rash that includes an identifying tattoo is a privacy breach even if the name is cropped out.
scenario: A student wants to post a teaching photo of a back rash. The frame includes a distinctive tattoo and the clinic hallway sign. The patient's name is not in the image. The patient was not asked. The case is rare enough that classmates would recognize the person.
question: Which use is allowed?
options: No posting without consent, tattoo included
Post it because the name is absent
Post it to a public gallery labeled teaching
Crop nothing and add the history
Send it to a class group chat
correctAnswer: No posting without consent, tattoo included
explanation: A photo of a rash that includes an identifying tattoo is a privacy breach even if the name is cropped out. No posting without consent, tattoo included is the limit, because the tattoo and the hallway identify him. Post it because the name is absent ignores other identifiers. Post it to a public gallery labeled teaching is still a disclosure. Crop nothing and add the history adds more identifiers. Send it to a class group chat is the same breach.

examTakeaway: A large gift from a device company, offered before a purchasing vote, is declined.
scenario: A 48-year-old surgeon is about to vote on which implant system the hospital will buy. The vendor offers an all-expenses weekend at a resort for the surgeon and a guest, tied to no educational program. A modest textbook from last year's conference is a separate, already-accepted item and is not this offer.
question: Which response fits the resort offer?
options: Ask the vendor to pay the hospital instead of disclosing
Accept if the guest stays home
Accept and disclose it after the vote
explanation: A large gift from a device company, offered before a purchasing vote, is declined. Decline the trip removes the influence. Accept and then vote lets the gift steer the choice. Accept if the guest stays home is still a large personal gift. Accept and disclose it after the vote discloses too late to protect the vote. Ask the vendor to pay the hospital instead of disclosing still ties money to the decision he is about to make.

examTakeaway: A patient who meets brain-death criteria is dead, and a family request does not restore the duty to continue organ support for the patient's sake.
scenario: A 30-year-old man has no brainstem reflexes on two exams, and the apnea test shows no breaths. The cause is known and confounding drugs have cleared. His parents ask that the ventilator continue because they believe he will wake. No religious objection procedure has been invoked. Organ donation has not been decided.
question: Which statement is accurate?
options: The parents can reverse the determination
One more day of support is medically required
explanation: A patient who meets brain-death criteria is dead, and a family request does not restore the duty to continue organ support for the patient's sake. He meets criteria for death when the exams and the apnea test agree and confounders are gone. The parents can reverse the determination is not true. One more day of support is medically required is not required for his sake once death is determined. The apnea test is optional is wrong; it is part of the examination. Sedation still explains the exam contradicts the cleared-drug finding.

examTakeaway: A signed donor card is the patient's gift, and the family is asked to honor it rather than to veto it.
scenario: A 22-year-old man is dead by neurologic criteria. His license has a signed donor authorization. His parents are grieving and at first say they do not want donation. The coordinator has not yet explained that he already authorized it. No evidence suggests the signature was forged.
question: Which fact leads the conversation?
explanation: A signed donor card is the patient's gift, and the family is asked to honor it rather than to veto it. He already authorized the gift, so the conversation starts there. The parents hold a veto is not the rule when his own authorization is valid. Donation requires a court order is not required for a signed authorization. Only a spouse can authorize ignores his own signature. The signature expired at admission is not how donor designation works.

examTakeaway: Relative risk is the incidence in the exposed divided by the incidence in the unexposed, from a cohort.
scenario: A 22-year-old student follows 200 smokers and 200 people who never smoked for 10 years. Lung cancer occurs in 20 smokers and in 4 never-smokers. No one is sampled because they already have cancer. She is asked for the relative risk.
question: Which number is the relative risk?
explanation: Relative risk is the incidence in the exposed divided by the incidence in the unexposed, from a cohort. 5 is 20/200 divided by 4/200. 4 is the count of cancers in never-smokers, not the ratio of rates. 16 would be an odds ratio miscomputed from these counts if someone multiplies the wrong cells. 0.2 is the inverse of the relative risk. 24 is the sum of the cancer counts, not a ratio.

examTakeaway: A very sensitive test that is negative makes the disease unlikely, which is why sensitivity rules out.
scenario: A 22-year-old student reads that a D-dimer assay is 98 percent sensitive and 40 percent specific for clot. A patient with a low pretest probability has a negative D-dimer. She must say what the negative result does.
question: Which conclusion fits the negative result?
options: The test is useless because specificity is 40 percent
The negative result raises the probability
explanation: A very sensitive test that is negative makes the disease unlikely, which is why sensitivity rules out. Clot is unlikely because a 98 percent sensitive test rarely misses the disease. Clot is confirmed would require a positive result on a specific test. The test is useless because specificity is 40 percent confuses the use of a negative result with the false alarms of a positive one. The negative result raises the probability is the wrong direction. Specificity is what cleared him is the wrong property; specificity governs false positives.

examTakeaway: Random assignment balances both known and unknown confounders between groups.
scenario: A 22-year-old student compares two designs. In one, clinicians choose who gets the new drug. In the other, a random number assigns the drug. Age, smoking, and unmeasured frailty worry her. She asks which design balances those differences.
question: Which design balances confounders?
options: Matching only on age after the fact in an uncontrolled series
explanation: Random assignment balances both known and unknown confounders between groups. Random assignment is the design that does it, including frailty she cannot measure. Letting clinicians choose puts sicker patients in one arm. A case series has no comparison arm. Matching only on age after the fact in an uncontrolled series does not balance unmeasured factors and is not randomization. Asking patients to pick recreates the same confounding.

examTakeaway: A study that enrolls only people who answer a clinic poster over-represents the worried and the well, which is selection bias.
scenario: A 22-year-old student reviews a survey of back pain. Subjects are people who saw a poster in a gym and volunteered. People who are bedridden with pain never saw the poster. The authors claim the sample represents all adults with back pain.
question: Which bias is this?
options: Observer bias from an unblinded reader
explanation: A study that enrolls only people who answer a clinic poster over-represents the worried and the well, which is selection bias. Selection bias is who got into the sample. Recall bias is how people remember exposures. Lead-time bias is an earlier clock from screening. Observer bias from an unblinded reader is how outcomes are judged, not who enrolled. Confounding by smoking is a third variable mixed with the exposure, which this poster story does not describe.

examTakeaway: A skewed income distribution is summarized by the median, because a few high values pull the mean.
scenario: A 22-year-old student has nine households earning 40,000 and one earning 2,000,000. She must report a single typical income. The mean is far above what most households earn. The distribution has a long right tail.
question: Which summary matches the typical household?
explanation: A skewed income distribution is summarized by the median, because a few high values pull the mean. The median stays at 40,000, where most households are. The mean is dragged up by the single large income. The mode of the million does not exist as a repeated value. The range describes spread, not the typical household. The standard deviation also describes spread.

examTakeaway: No social smile by three months is a reason to examine hearing and vision, not a normal variant to watch until the first birthday.
scenario: A 4-month-old does not smile at a face and does not watch the parent cross the room. Birth was at term and there was no jaundice severe enough to cause worry at the time. The parents were told to wait until the first birthday. Weight gain is normal.
question: Which response fits the missing smile?
options: Start speech therapy as the only step
explanation: No social smile by three months is a reason to examine hearing and vision, not a normal variant to watch until the first birthday. Check hearing and vision now, because a sensory loss can look like a social delay and the smile should already be present. Wait until age 1 misses months of a sensory problem. Start speech therapy as the only step skips the sensory exam in an infant who is not yet at speech age. Diagnose autism today is too early and skips hearing and vision. Order a brain biopsy is not the opening test.

examTakeaway: A 9-month-old who cannot sit with support is delayed, because unsupported or supported sitting is expected well before then.
scenario: A 9-month-old boy cannot sit even when his trunk is held. He does not babble. He rolled at 4 months and then progress stopped. Birth was at term. The parents think boys sit late and want to wait until age 2. Hearing has not been tested.
question: Which finding is the delay?
options: Not sitting with support at 9 months
correctAnswer: Not sitting with support at 9 months
explanation: A 9-month-old who cannot sit with support is delayed, because unsupported or supported sitting is expected well before then. Not sitting with support at 9 months is the delay, and the lost progress after rolling adds to it. Rolling at 4 months was on time and is not the problem. Wanting to wait is the parents' plan, not a developmental finding. A normal birth does not explain the stall. Male sex is not a reason to miss sitting at 9 months.
